screens.title: High Availability and Redundancy Strategies
screens.narratorSegment: High availability is the art of keeping a system operational and accessible despite failures. In distributed design this becomes a practice: you identify single points of failure, add redundancy, and provide automated failover so users keep working. You will learn core redundancy patterns — active-passive, active-active, and N+1 — and when to choose each. You will also see how replication, load balancing, health checks, and geographic distribution work together to reduce downtime and data loss. For example, a cluster of stateless web servers behind a load balancer is a classic active-active setup that maintains service when an instance dies. By contrast, a primary database with a streaming replica is often active-passive, trading simplicity for some recovery time. Throughout this lesson we will focus on practical trade-offs: cost versus recovery time, consistency versus latency, and the operational complexity each pattern introduces. Think about your critical component and ask: what is its acceptable downtime, and what level of complexity can my team operate? That question will guide every HA choice you make.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.2 › High Availability
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

High Availability & Redundancy

Understand patterns and mechanisms that keep services available despite failures. Learn practical trade-offs and design steps to eliminate single points of failure.

In this lesson
Hands-on scenario
Why this matters

Downtime hurts users and revenue. Designing HA means balancing cost, recovery time, and operational complexity. This lesson gives concrete patterns and checks you can apply right away.

Redundancy
Duplicate critical components so one fails and another can continue.
Replication
Copy data across nodes to protect durability and enable recovery.
Failover
Detect failures and switch automatically to healthy components.
Concept Map
Stateless Pool
Multiple instances behind a load balancer provide seamless failover for web servers.
Ideal for horizontal scaling and active-active setups.
Stateful DB
Primary with replica(s) needs replication and promotion logic for failover.
Often uses active-passive replication for consistency.
Coming up
We will compare strategies, inspect trade-offs, and design an HA solution for an order processing microservice with PostgreSQL.
Explore Key Topics
Redundancy Patterns
Active-passive, active-active, and N+1 — when to choose each based on recovery time and complexity.
Replication Models
Synchronous vs asynchronous replication and the consistency-latency trade-off.
Detection & Failover
Health checks, watchdogs, and automated promotion to reduce human intervention.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will be able to identify critical components that need redundancy, select appropriate redundancy strategies, and implement common mechanisms like load balancing, replication, and automated failover. First, you will understand the fundamental principles of high availability and why eliminating single points of failure is more than adding extra servers. Second, you will be able to differentiate active-passive, active-active, and N+1 redundancy and match them to concrete use cases. Third, you will deploy load balancers, design health checks, and describe failover procedures so system availability responds automatically to failures. Finally, you will analyze trade-offs between cost, complexity, recovery time, and consistency, and design an HA architecture for a critical microservice and its database. Each objective includes a practical milestone to verify competency, such as drafting an active-passive failover plan for a database or specifying a health check policy for a microservice. These skills are immediately useful when reviewing architecture diagrams, running failure drills, or answering system design interview questions about availability.

screens.title: What is High Availability (HA)?
screens.narratorSegment: High availability means that a system remains operational and accessible for a required time window, minimizing downtime and service interruption. The goal is not to prevent every failure—failures happen—but to ensure the system can continue performing its intended function with little or no interruption. A common first step is identifying single points of failure: components whose outage would stop the whole system. Eliminating SPOFs typically involves introducing redundancy and failover mechanisms. For example, a single database server is a SPOF; adding a replica and a promotion process reduces risk. A misconception is to assume simply adding more instances guarantees HA. Without health checks, proper replication, and clear failover logic, multiple instances may all fail to recover automatically. A concrete example is a stateless web tier: by deploying multiple instances behind a load balancer, requests continue to be served even when one instance fails, provided the load balancer properly checks instance health. Key takeaway: HA is design discipline—identify critical components, decide acceptable downtime and data loss, then apply redundancy and detection to meet those goals. How available does your system need to be and what failures do you plan for?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: HA is the system's capacity to operate through failures by removing SPOFs and enabling automated recovery.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.2 › What is HA?
Core Concept

High Availability

An operational goal: systems remain available for the required period despite component failures.

Key properties
  • Eliminate single points of failure by adding redundant components.
  • Detect failures with reliable health checks and switch automatically.
  • Accept that failures occur and design graceful recovery paths.
Common misconception
More instances alone are not sufficient. Without replication consistency and failover automation, redundancy may not improve availability.
Key Takeaway

Treat HA as a design process: identify SPOFs, pick redundancy strategies, implement detection and failover, then test repeatedly.

Example Scenario
A single primary database is promoted to a replica on failure. The system must ensure replication keeps the standby up-to-date and a watchdog promotes the replica quickly to minimize downtime.
Check your understanding
Name one component in your stack that would be a SPOF and state whether you would use active-passive, active-active, or N+1 to remove the SPOF and why.

screens.title: Replication: stateless vs stateful components
screens.narratorSegment: Replication is the practice of maintaining multiple copies of data or service instances so that a failure does not cause data loss or downtime. For stateless services replication is straightforward: run multiple instances and place a load balancer in front. Requests are routed to healthy instances and state is stored elsewhere, removing the need to coordinate writes. For stateful components like databases, replication is more complex because you must preserve data consistency across replicas. Databases often use primary-standby streaming replication where the primary sends write-ahead logs to replicas. That makes failover simpler because only one writer exists at a time, reducing consistency headaches. Alternatively, multi-master or multi-region active-active databases allow writes in multiple locations but require conflict resolution or distributed consensus, which increases complexity. A useful mental model: for stateless services, replication is horizontal scaling; for stateful systems, replication is careful choreography between nodes. Misconception: treating a stateful replica as if it were instantly writable without promotion logic. Always design replication with explicit promotion and consistency policies. Takeaway: choose replication appropriate to the component’s statefulness and the system’s tolerance for complexity and possible data loss.

keyIdea.text: Stateless services scale by instance replication behind load balancers; stateful systems need replication strategies that preserve consistency and support promotion.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.2 › Replication
Architecture

Stateless vs Stateful Replication

Understand replication patterns and the operational work needed to keep replicas correct and promotable.

Stateless service replication
Deploy multiple identical instances. Use a load balancer to route requests and remove unhealthy instances. No coordination for writes is required because state is external.
Stateful replication
Use streaming replication or multi-master approaches. Synchronous replication gives stronger guarantees; asynchronous trades durability for latency.
Concrete example
Web servers: multiple instances behind a cloud load balancer. Database: primary with continuous WAL streaming to a replica. Promotion requires a watchdog or orchestration tool to update connection endpoints.
Common mistake
Assuming a replica can accept writes immediately. Stateful replicas commonly require promotion to become the primary writer to avoid split-brain or data corruption.
Key Takeaway

Match replication approach to component type: simple replication for stateless, explicit promotion and consistency controls for stateful.

screens.title: Active-Passive (Primary-Standby)
screens.narratorSegment: Active-passive setups have a single active component handling all traffic while one or more passive standbys receive updates and wait to take over if the active fails. This pattern simplifies consistency because only one node accepts writes, so the failover process focuses on promotion and ensuring the standby is up-to-date. An example is a primary PostgreSQL server with streaming replication to a replica. Pros of active-passive include easier data consistency management and simpler failover logic. Cons are underutilized standby capacity and potentially higher recovery time as the standby initializes and assumes the active role, which increases the recovery time objective. Use active-passive when strict consistency is required and brief outages during failover are acceptable. A common misconception is to rely on periodic snapshot replication without verifying the replica’s readiness; that can lead to outdated standbys and longer recovery. The practical checklist: keep replication lag low, automate promotion with a watchdog such as Patroni or similar tooling, and ensure connection endpoints update promptly during failover. The final question to consider: how much failover downtime is acceptable for your component? Active-Passive (Primary-Standby) means one active writer and standby replicas reduce consistency complexity but trade off utilization and recovery time.. In practical terms, simple failover with one active writer and standby replicas. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.2 › Active-Passive
Comparison

Active-Passive Pattern

One active node handles traffic; passive standby receives updates and is promoted on failure.

Pros
Simpler consistency; single writer avoids multi-master conflicts.
Cons
Standby underutilized and failover may introduce a brief outage during promotion.
Concrete Example
A primary PostgreSQL streams WAL to a replica. On primary failure, a watchdog promotes the replica and updates DNS or connection strings to point clients to the new primary.
Common-mistake

Failing to test promotion and connection reconfiguration. Without rehearsed procedures, failover can take much longer than expected.

Key Takeaway

Use active-passive for strong consistency needs, but automate and test promotion to reduce RTO.

screens.title: Active-Active deployments
screens.narratorSegment: Active-active configurations run multiple redundant components that all accept traffic simultaneously. This improves utilization and often provides zero downtime during node failures because traffic simply shifts to the remaining healthy instances. It’s a natural fit for stateless services like web servers and A P I gateways. However, for stateful systems active-active introduces complexity because multiple writers require coordination — either conflict resolution, distributed consensus, or eventual consistency models. For multi-region deployments, active-active can deliver better performance by routing users to the nearest healthy region, but it requires global routing and careful testing for data reconciliation. A common example is a fleet of identical web servers behind a load balancer. The load balancer distributes incoming requests and removes unhealthy targets based on health checks. Misconception: active-active magically prevents all outages. If you deploy a buggy configuration to all active nodes, the whole system can fail. Operational practices such as gradual rollouts and circuit breakers are essential. The takeaway: active-active reduces downtime risk at the cost of higher operational and consistency complexity. Active-Active deployments means multiple nodes accept traffic for better utilization and seamless failover, but stateful multi-writer setups need coordination or conflict resolution.. In practical terms, higher utilization and seamless failover with more complexity. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.2 › Active-Active
Architecture

Active-Active Deployments

All redundant components are simultaneously active and handling requests, often behind a load balancer.

When to use
Stateless services, API gateways, and read-scalable stores where multi-writer complexity is unacceptable.
Operational needs
Robust health checks, gradual deployment strategies, and protections against simultaneous misconfiguration.
Concrete example
Multiple web servers in several regions behind global load balancing. Traffic is routed to nearest healthy region and shifted automatically on outages.
Common-mistake

Assuming active-active removes the need for careful rollouts. A faulty change pushed everywhere can still take the whole system down.

Key Takeaway

Active-active minimizes downtime but requires strong operational practices and careful design for stateful components.

screens.title: N+1 Redundancy
screens.narratorSegment: N+1 redundancy means you provision N active components and at least one spare to take over if any active unit fails. It is a practical compromise between full duplication and no redundancy: you avoid dedicating a standby per active node while still protecting against an individual failure. This model works well for server clusters, power supplies, and network devices where a single spare can cover the failure of any active unit. The key operational step is capacity planning — the spare must be able to carry the load of a failed unit, and you must monitor aggregate load to ensure headroom. A common pitfall is underestimating peak load or ignoring multiple simultaneous failures; N+1 protects against only a single unit outage. For example, a cluster of five application servers with one spare can tolerate one failure without scaling events, but two simultaneous failures will require autoscaling or will impact performance. The takeaway is to match N+1 to your failure model and ensure monitoring and autoscaling policies are in place to handle second-order events. N+1 Redundancy means provision one spare to cover a single unit failure; plan capacity and monitoring so the spare can carry the load when needed.. In practical terms, efficient spare capacity planning. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.2 › N+1 Redundancy
Process Flow

N+1 Redundancy

An efficient redundancy model meaning N active units plus at least one spare that can take over if any single unit fails.

When to use
Clusters where one spare can cover a failed node, and tight resource utilization is required.
Operational checklist
Ensure spare capacity is tested, monitor cluster load, and configure autoscaling for multiple failures.
Limitation
Covers only one failure; multiple failures require additional spares or autoscaling strategies.
Key Takeaway

N+1 balances fault tolerance and efficiency. Validate that the spare can handle the load of any single active node before relying on this model.

Example
Five application nodes plus one spare allows the system to tolerate one failure without performance loss.

screens.title: Load Balancing and Algorithms
screens.narratorSegment: Load balancers distribute incoming traffic across multiple servers to avoid overloading any single node and to enable seamless failover. They operate at different network layers: Layer 4 load balancers route by IP and port, while Layer 7 load balancers can inspect HTTP and route requests by headers or path. Common algorithms include round-robin, which equally shares requests; least-connections, which favors underloaded servers; and IP-hash, which steers a client to a particular backend for session affinity. Choosing the right algorithm depends on request patterns and session behavior. For long-lived connections, least-connections reduces hot spots; for simple stateless requests, round-robin is often sufficient. Health checks are central: the load balancer must confirm that a backend responds correctly before sending traffic. Misconfiguration of health checks can lead to routing traffic to unhealthy nodes or mistakenly draining healthy ones. A concrete example: an A P I gateway using least-connections for long-polling requests while a CDN front-end uses IP-hash to keep client sessions consistent. Takeaway: design load-balancer settings and health checks that match application characteristics to support HA effectively. Load Balancing and Algorithms means choose a layer and algorithm that match your traffic and session characteristics, and pair with accurate health checks.. In practical terms, how traffic distribution supports availability. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.2 › Load Balancing
Process Flow

Load Balancer Choices

Pick L4 or L7 and an algorithm based on connection patterns and session needs.

Algorithms
Round-robin, least-connections, IP-hash. Match algorithm to request type and connection lifetime.
Health checks
Use readiness and liveness checks to ensure only healthy backends receive traffic. Include dependency verification when necessary.
Example
An API gateway uses least-connections because requests are long-lived, while a static content service can use round-robin for even distribution.
Common-mistake

Using health checks that only verify network reachability, not application readiness. This sends traffic to servers that are not ready to serve requests.

Key Takeaway

Align load-balancer behavior and health checks with how your application handles connections and dependencies to maintain availability.

screens.title: Failover and Health Checks
screens.narratorSegment: Failover is the automated process that moves traffic or responsibilities from a failed component to a healthy one. Reliable failover begins with health checks that accurately reflect operational readiness, not just network reachability. Design health checks that exercise critical functionality, such as connecting to a database or verifying a cache. For databases, a watchdog should verify both connectivity and replication health before promoting a standby. For stateless services, a readiness endpoint can indicate when the instance has loaded necessary dependencies. When a health check fails, the system can update load balancer target groups, change DNS records (respecting TTL), or trigger a promotion workflow. A typical failure sequence includes detection, isolation (draining traffic), promotion or rerouting, and verification. Misconception: treating a single successful ping as sufficient. Health checks should include short, meaningful work that proves the service can handle production requests. Concrete example: implement an HTTP /health endpoint that performs a lightweight database query to confirm the app and its dependency are responsive. Key takeaway: automated, realistic health checks plus tested promotion steps are essential to keep recovery fast and reliable.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.2 › Failover & Health Checks
Process Flow

Failover Sequence

Detect failure, isolate the bad node, reroute traffic, promote standby if needed, and verify the system is healthy.

Design health checks
Include dependency checks and lightweight operations to reflect real readiness.
Automate promotion
Use a watchdog or orchestration tool to promote replicas and update endpoints without manual steps.
Concrete example
Expose an HTTP readiness endpoint that performs a small database query. The load balancer removes instances that fail this check and the watchdog promotes a replica if the primary is unreachable.
Common-mistake

Using only network-level pings as health checks. Those do not prove application-level readiness and cause false positives.

Key Takeaway

Test and automate failover steps. Realistic health checks are the foundation of reliable recovery.

screens.title: Synchronous vs Asynchronous Replication
screens.narratorSegment: Synchronous and asynchronous replication trade off consistency and latency. Synchronous replication waits for data to be written to replicas before acknowledging a write to the client. This ensures strong consistency and zero data loss in many failure scenarios, but it increases write latency and can reduce throughput because the primary must wait for acknowledgments. Asynchronous replication acknowledges the write immediately on the primary and then streams changes to replicas later; this improves latency and throughput but risks some data loss if the primary fails before replication completes. Choose synchronous replication when zero data loss is essential, such as financial transactions or critical inventory updates. Choose asynchronous replication when low latency and high write throughput matter more than absolute durability, for example in analytics ingestion or logging. A common mistake is enabling synchronous replication without understanding the latency impact under network partitions. Always measure write latency with your chosen replication mode and document acceptable recovery point objectives. The practical step: map each data type to an RPO and choose replication mode accordingly. Synchronous vs Asynchronous Replication means synchronous favors consistency and zero data loss at the cost of latency; asynchronous favors low latency and throughput but allows potential data loss.. In practical terms, consistency, latency, and when to choose each. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 8 › Chapter 8.2 › Sync vs Async
Definition

Synchronous vs Asynchronous

Understand the consistency-latency trade-off to choose replication mode by data criticality.

Synchronous
Write acknowledged only after replicas confirm; strong consistency, higher latency.
Asynchronous
Primary acknowledges write immediately; lower latency but potential for data loss on failure.
When to choose
Synchronous for financial or critical operations with zero tolerance for loss; asynchronous for high-throughput, latency-sensitive workloads.
Common-mistake

Enabling synchronous replication across distant regions without accounting for network latency, which can dramatically slow writes.

Key Takeaway

Map data to RPO requirements and choose replication mode so critical data uses stronger durability while less-critical data favors performance.

screens.title: Geographic Redundancy and Multi-Region
screens.narratorSegment: Geographic redundancy deploys systems across multiple availability zones or regions to protect against large-scale outages and improve latency by serving users from nearby locations. You can operate regions in active-active mode to distribute traffic by proximity, or active-passive mode where a secondary region stands ready to take over. Global load balancing and DNS routing with health checks are essential to detect region failures and redirect traffic to healthy locations. Multi-region deployments introduce consistency challenges: either accept eventual consistency, use conflict resolution, or implement distributed consensus, which increases complexity. Another key operational concern is DNS TTL: long TTLs delay failover while very short TTLs increase global DNS query load. A common mistake is assuming multi-region deployment removes the need for local health checks and failover logic; each region should be resilient on its own. Concrete example: deploy stateless services in active-active across regions, while keeping a single-writer database replicated appropriately or using region-aware databases. Takeaway: multi-region architecture increases availability and performance but requires deliberate replication and routing strategies. Geographic Redundancy and Multi-Region means deploy across azs or regions and combine global routing with local resilience; plan for consistency and dns behavior.. In practical terms, protecting against data-center or region-wide failures. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.2 › Geographic Redundancy
Architecture

Multi-Region Deployments

Use multiple availability zones or regions with global routing to minimize blast radius and improve latency.

Active-Active multi-region
Serve users from the nearest region and failover with global routing. Requires reconciliation for multi-writer data models.
Active-Passive multi-region
Secondary region stands ready to take over. Easier data consistency but longer RTO on region failover.
DNS considerations
Balance DNS TTL to trade faster failover against global DNS load and cache behavior.
Operational note
Each region must itself be resilient. Multi-region does not replace proper local redundancy and health checks.

screens.title: Designing HA for an Order Processing Microservice
screens.narratorSegment: Now apply what you've learned to a concrete scenario: an order processing microservice with a PostgreSQL database. For the database, active-passive is a common choice. Use streaming replication where the primary ships write-ahead logs to a replica. Implement a watchdog that performs regular health checks — connectivity, last received WAL position, disk health — and promotes the replica if the primary fails. Ensure automated updates to connection strings or DNS so clients reconnect to the new primary. For the microservice itself, use active-active: deploy multiple instances across availability zones behind a load balancer. Implement an HTTP readiness endpoint that verifies the service can reach the database and other dependencies. Choose the load-balancer algorithm based on request patterns; least-connections is often useful for long-running order workflows. Define health checks so the load balancer removes unhealthy instances quickly. Finally, document RTO and RPO: choose synchronous replication for orders only if zero data loss is mandatory; otherwise use asynchronous replication with low-lag monitoring. A common pitfall is failing to rehearse failover. Schedule drills to validate promotion, DNS updates, and client reconnection behaviors. Question: what RPO and RTO targets will you set for orders in your business context?

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.2 › Order Processing HA
Hands-on Activity

Order Processing Microservice

Design a resilient service with a highly available PostgreSQL and multiple service instances.

Database (Active-Passive)
Use streaming replication. A watchdog monitors WAL lag and connectivity. On primary failure the replica is promoted and clients are redirected to updated connection endpoints.
Microservice (Active-Active)
Deploy multiple instances across AZs behind a load balancer. Expose a readiness endpoint that verifies DB connectivity and remove unhealthy nodes automatically.
Health checks & testing
Define realistic health probes and rehearse failover drills to validate promotion and client reconnection behaviors.
Starter Template
Service: Order Processing Microservice with PostgreSQL

1. PostgreSQL (Active-Passive):
   * Replication Mechanism: Use PostgreSQL's streaming replication. The primary streams its write-ahead log to a replica.
   * Failover Mechanism: Implement a watchdog (e.g., Patroni or similar) that monitors the primary. If the primary fails, promote the replica, update DNS/connection strings, and start a new replica if needed.

2. Order Processing Microservice (Active-Active):
   * Redundancy Strategy: Deploy multiple instances across availability zones.
   * Request Distribution: Place a cloud load balancer in front and use least-connections for long-running requests.

3. Health Checks:
   * Microservice: Expose an HTTP /health that verifies DB connectivity and dependencies.
   * Database: Watchdog periodically runs a simple SELECT 1 and checks WAL streaming status on the replica.
Key Takeaway

Document RTO/RPO and rehearse failover. Practical testing is the final and essential step of HA design.

Load Balancer
Routes traffic and enforces health checks to prevent overloaded or unhealthy servers from receiving requests.
Failover
Automated switching to healthy components when failures are detected, minimizing manual steps.
Health Check

fullNarratorScript:
High availability is the art of keeping a system operational and accessible despite failures. In distributed design this becomes a practice: you identify single points of failure, add redundancy, and provide automated failover so users keep working. You will learn core redundancy patterns — active-passive, active-active, and N+1 — and when to choose each. You will also see how replication, load balancing, health checks, and geographic distribution work together to reduce downtime and data loss. For example, a cluster of stateless web servers behind a load balancer is a classic active-active setup that maintains service when an instance dies. By contrast, a primary database with a streaming replica is often active-passive, trading simplicity for some recovery time. Throughout this lesson we will focus on practical trade-offs: cost versus recovery time, consistency versus latency, and the operational complexity each pattern introduces. Think about your critical component and ask: what is its acceptable downtime, and what level of complexity can my team operate? That question will guide every HA choice you make.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to identify critical components that need redundancy, select appropriate redundancy strategies, and implement common mechanisms like load balancing, replication, and automated failover. First, you will understand the fundamental principles of high availability and why eliminating single points of failure is more than adding extra servers. Second, you will be able to differentiate active-passive, active-active, and N+1 redundancy and match them to concrete use cases. Third, you will deploy load balancers, design health checks, and describe failover procedures so system availability responds automatically to failures. Finally, you will analyze trade-offs between cost, complexity, recovery time, and consistency, and design an HA architecture for a critical microservice and its database. Each objective includes a practical milestone to verify competency, such as drafting an active-passive failover plan for a database or specifying a health check policy for a microservice. These skills are immediately useful when reviewing architecture diagrams, running failure drills, or answering system design interview questions about availability.

This second objectives slide focuses on mechanisms and trade-offs you will master. You will learn how load balancers operate at different layers and choose algorithms that match traffic patterns. You will design health checks that accurately reflect application readiness, and learn how failover procedures update DNS, target groups, or promote replicas. You will also compare synchronous and asynchronous replication, so you can choose strong consistency when zero data loss matters or choose lower latency when throughput is paramount. Finally, you will understand multi-region strategies to protect against data center failures and how global routing can direct users to the nearest healthy region. For verification, you will create sample health check definitions and a replication policy that states when synchronous replication is required and where asynchronous is acceptable. These objectives tie the theoretical patterns to operational steps you can implement and test with failure drills.

High availability means that a system remains operational and accessible for a required time window, minimizing downtime and service interruption. The goal is not to prevent every failure—failures happen—but to ensure the system can continue performing its intended function with little or no interruption. A common first step is identifying single points of failure: components whose outage would stop the whole system. Eliminating SPOFs typically involves introducing redundancy and failover mechanisms. For example, a single database server is a SPOF; adding a replica and a promotion process reduces risk. A misconception is to assume simply adding more instances guarantees HA. Without health checks, proper replication, and clear failover logic, multiple instances may all fail to recover automatically. A concrete example is a stateless web tier: by deploying multiple instances behind a load balancer, requests continue to be served even when one instance fails, provided the load balancer properly checks instance health. Key takeaway: HA is design discipline—identify critical components, decide acceptable downtime and data loss, then apply redundancy and detection to meet those goals. How available does your system need to be and what failures do you plan for?

Replication is the practice of maintaining multiple copies of data or service instances so that a failure does not cause data loss or downtime. For stateless services replication is straightforward: run multiple instances and place a load balancer in front. Requests are routed to healthy instances and state is stored elsewhere, removing the need to coordinate writes. For stateful components like databases, replication is more complex because you must preserve data consistency across replicas. Databases often use primary-standby streaming replication where the primary sends write-ahead logs to replicas. That makes failover simpler because only one writer exists at a time, reducing consistency headaches. Alternatively, multi-master or multi-region active-active databases allow writes in multiple locations but require conflict resolution or distributed consensus, which increases complexity. A useful mental model: for stateless services, replication is horizontal scaling; for stateful systems, replication is careful choreography between nodes. Misconception: treating a stateful replica as if it were instantly writable without promotion logic. Always design replication with explicit promotion and consistency policies. Takeaway: choose replication appropriate to the component’s statefulness and the system’s tolerance for complexity and possible data loss.

Active-passive setups have a single active component handling all traffic while one or more passive standbys receive updates and wait to take over if the active fails. This pattern simplifies consistency because only one node accepts writes, so the failover process focuses on promotion and ensuring the standby is up-to-date. An example is a primary PostgreSQL server with streaming replication to a replica. Pros of active-passive include easier data consistency management and simpler failover logic. Cons are underutilized standby capacity and potentially higher recovery time as the standby initializes and assumes the active role, which increases the recovery time objective. Use active-passive when strict consistency is required and brief outages during failover are acceptable. A common misconception is to rely on periodic snapshot replication without verifying the replica’s readiness; that can lead to outdated standbys and longer recovery. The practical checklist: keep replication lag low, automate promotion with a watchdog such as Patroni or similar tooling, and ensure connection endpoints update promptly during failover. The final question to consider: how much failover downtime is acceptable for your component? Active-Passive (Primary-Standby) means one active writer and standby replicas reduce consistency complexity but trade off utilization and recovery time.. In practical terms, simple failover with one active writer and standby replicas. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Active-active configurations run multiple redundant components that all accept traffic simultaneously. This improves utilization and often provides zero downtime during node failures because traffic simply shifts to the remaining healthy instances. It’s a natural fit for stateless services like web servers and A P I gateways. However, for stateful systems active-active introduces complexity because multiple writers require coordination — either conflict resolution, distributed consensus, or eventual consistency models. For multi-region deployments, active-active can deliver better performance by routing users to the nearest healthy region, but it requires global routing and careful testing for data reconciliation. A common example is a fleet of identical web servers behind a load balancer. The load balancer distributes incoming requests and removes unhealthy targets based on health checks. Misconception: active-active magically prevents all outages. If you deploy a buggy configuration to all active nodes, the whole system can fail. Operational practices such as gradual rollouts and circuit breakers are essential. The takeaway: active-active reduces downtime risk at the cost of higher operational and consistency complexity. Active-Active deployments means multiple nodes accept traffic for better utilization and seamless failover, but stateful multi-writer setups need coordination or conflict resolution.. In practical terms, higher utilization and seamless failover with more complexity. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

N+1 redundancy means you provision N active components and at least one spare to take over if any active unit fails. It is a practical compromise between full duplication and no redundancy: you avoid dedicating a standby per active node while still protecting against an individual failure. This model works well for server clusters, power supplies, and network devices where a single spare can cover the failure of any active unit. The key operational step is capacity planning — the spare must be able to carry the load of a failed unit, and you must monitor aggregate load to ensure headroom. A common pitfall is underestimating peak load or ignoring multiple simultaneous failures; N+1 protects against only a single unit outage. For example, a cluster of five application servers with one spare can tolerate one failure without scaling events, but two simultaneous failures will require autoscaling or will impact performance. The takeaway is to match N+1 to your failure model and ensure monitoring and autoscaling policies are in place to handle second-order events. N+1 Redundancy means provision one spare to cover a single unit failure; plan capacity and monitoring so the spare can carry the load when needed.. In practical terms, efficient spare capacity planning. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Load balancers distribute incoming traffic across multiple servers to avoid overloading any single node and to enable seamless failover. They operate at different network layers: Layer 4 load balancers route by IP and port, while Layer 7 load balancers can inspect HTTP and route requests by headers or path. Common algorithms include round-robin, which equally shares requests; least-connections, which favors underloaded servers; and IP-hash, which steers a client to a particular backend for session affinity. Choosing the right algorithm depends on request patterns and session behavior. For long-lived connections, least-connections reduces hot spots; for simple stateless requests, round-robin is often sufficient. Health checks are central: the load balancer must confirm that a backend responds correctly before sending traffic. Misconfiguration of health checks can lead to routing traffic to unhealthy nodes or mistakenly draining healthy ones. A concrete example: an A P I gateway using least-connections for long-polling requests while a CDN front-end uses IP-hash to keep client sessions consistent. Takeaway: design load-balancer settings and health checks that match application characteristics to support HA effectively. Load Balancing and Algorithms means choose a layer and algorithm that match your traffic and session characteristics, and pair with accurate health checks.. In practical terms, how traffic distribution supports availability. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Failover is the automated process that moves traffic or responsibilities from a failed component to a healthy one. Reliable failover begins with health checks that accurately reflect operational readiness, not just network reachability. Design health checks that exercise critical functionality, such as connecting to a database or verifying a cache. For databases, a watchdog should verify both connectivity and replication health before promoting a standby. For stateless services, a readiness endpoint can indicate when the instance has loaded necessary dependencies. When a health check fails, the system can update load balancer target groups, change DNS records (respecting TTL), or trigger a promotion workflow. A typical failure sequence includes detection, isolation (draining traffic), promotion or rerouting, and verification. Misconception: treating a single successful ping as sufficient. Health checks should include short, meaningful work that proves the service can handle production requests. Concrete example: implement an HTTP /health endpoint that performs a lightweight database query to confirm the app and its dependency are responsive. Key takeaway: automated, realistic health checks plus tested promotion steps are essential to keep recovery fast and reliable.

Synchronous and asynchronous replication trade off consistency and latency. Synchronous replication waits for data to be written to replicas before acknowledging a write to the client. This ensures strong consistency and zero data loss in many failure scenarios, but it increases write latency and can reduce throughput because the primary must wait for acknowledgments. Asynchronous replication acknowledges the write immediately on the primary and then streams changes to replicas later; this improves latency and throughput but risks some data loss if the primary fails before replication completes. Choose synchronous replication when zero data loss is essential, such as financial transactions or critical inventory updates. Choose asynchronous replication when low latency and high write throughput matter more than absolute durability, for example in analytics ingestion or logging. A common mistake is enabling synchronous replication without understanding the latency impact under network partitions. Always measure write latency with your chosen replication mode and document acceptable recovery point objectives. The practical step: map each data type to an RPO and choose replication mode accordingly. Geographic redundancy deploys systems across multiple availability zones or regions to protect against large-scale outages and improve latency by serving users from nearby locations. You can operate regions in active-active mode to distribute traffic by proximity, or active-passive mode where a secondary region stands ready to take over. Global load balancing and DNS routing with health checks are essential to detect region failures and redirect traffic to healthy locations. Multi-region deployments introduce consistency challenges: either accept eventual consistency, use conflict resolution, or implement distributed consensus, which increases complexity. Another key operational concern is DNS TTL: long TTLs delay failover while very short TTLs increase global DNS query load. A common mistake is assuming multi-region deployment removes the need for local health checks and failover logic; each region should be resilient on its own. Concrete example: deploy stateless services in active-active across regions, while keeping a single-writer database replicated appropriately or using region-aware databases. Takeaway: multi-region architecture increases availability and performance but requires deliberate replication and routing strategies. Now apply what you've learned to a concrete scenario: an order processing microservice with a PostgreSQL database. For the database, active-passive is a common choice. Use streaming replication where the primary ships write-ahead logs to a replica. Implement a watchdog that performs regular health checks — connectivity, last received WAL position, disk health — and promotes the replica if the primary fails. Ensure automated updates to connection strings or DNS so clients reconnect to the new primary. For the microservice itself, use active-active: deploy multiple instances across availability zones behind a load balancer. Implement an HTTP readiness endpoint that verifies the service can reach the database and other dependencies. Choose the load-balancer algorithm based on request patterns; least-connections is often useful for long-running order workflows. Define health checks so the load balancer removes unhealthy instances quickly. Finally, document RTO and RPO: choose synchronous replication for orders only if zero data loss is mandatory; otherwise use asynchronous replication with low-lag monitoring. A common pitfall is failing to rehearse failover. Schedule drills to validate promotion, DNS updates, and client reconnection behaviors. These core concepts are your mental checklist when evaluating availability: High availability is the system’s ability to remain operational through failures. A single point of failure is any component whose failure stops the system; find and remove or mitigate it. Redundancy provides duplicate components to take over when failures occur. Active-passive simplifies consistency by having one writer with standbys, while active-active increases utilization but adds coordination challenges. N+1 gives efficient spare capacity to handle a single unit failure. Keep these definitions in mind when designing, because they guide your replication choices, health checks, and failover automation. Ask yourself: which components are critical, what downtime is acceptable, and what complexity can your team manage? Those answers drive the right redundancy pattern.
